<reflection>
The high-catalyst experiment differentiated mechanisms significantly. Leaders now are: M16 (-41.84), M5 (-40.95), M14 (-40.94), M11 (-40.68), M4 (-40.65), M20 (-40.12), M3 (-39.83), M17 (-38.85), M9 (-38.70). The gap between best and worst has grown substantially. Mechanisms suggesting substrate-related deactivation (M16, M11, M14) or unusual kinetic behavior (M5) fit better. Simple mechanisms M1, M2, M13, M15, M19 fit worst. This suggests catalyst deactivation is occurring, likely substrate-related or during turnover.

<hypothesis>
**Hypothesis discrimination**: The leaders (M16, M5, M14, M11) all involve substrate or turnover-related deactivation:
- M11: S+cat → inactive_catS (substrate deactivates free cat)
- M16: S+catS → inactive_catS2 (substrate deactivates bound catalyst)
- M14: catS → inactive_catS (spontaneous deactivation of bound cat, independent of [S])
- M5: additional catP intermediate—not deactivation but a different pathway
- M4: alternative catalytic species X

To distinguish substrate-dependent (M11, M16) vs. substrate-independent (M14) deactivation, run at LOW substrate concentration. M11/M16 predict LESS deactivation (higher conversion), M14 predicts SAME fractional deactivation. Also, M4 (X as second catalyst) predicts unusual scaling.

**Experiment design**: Low substrate (0.2 M), moderate catalyst (0.01 M), no product. This tests substrate-dependence of deactivation.

**Contrastive predictions**:
- M11: k3·[S]·[cat] deactivation slows at low [S]; near-complete conversion.
- M16: k3·[S]·[catS] deactivation slows; near-complete conversion. Both S-dependent inhibitors predict good conversion.
- M14: k3·[catS] deactivation—still fast during turnover; same fraction lost relative to turnovers—conversion may still be incomplete.
- M5: catP pathway—no deactivation, complete conversion, no dependence on [S] pattern.
- M4: X-catalyzed—rate depends differently on [S].
- M17: P-dependent deactivation—no P initially, some accumulates; conversion depends on how much P forms.
- M9, M20: cat-only deactivation—still occurs regardless of [S].
</hypothesis>
